title: Three Air India Passengers Skipped Immigration in Delhi, Ministry Issues Notice
excerpt: Three Italian nationals flew from Amritsar to Munich via Delhi without clearing immigration after airline staff funneled them through the wrong transfer route, prompting a show-cause notice from the civil aviation ministry.
body:
• Three Italian nationals flew from Amritsar to Munich via Delhi on September 4 without passing through mandatory immigration checks at Indira Gandhi International Airport.
  • The passengers arrived on Air India flight AI-1115 at about 12:50 am and boarded Lufthansa flight LH-763 to Munich at around 1:45 am, roughly an hour later.
  • The civil aviation ministry issued a show-cause notice to Air India on September 13, calling it a serious security and immigration-related lapse and giving the airline seven days to respond.
  • The breach stemmed from confusion around Air India's "Easy Connect" hub-and-spoke system: the passengers were not eligible for the fast-track transfer but were directed through the international transfer route anyway.

NEW DELHI — Three Italian nationals flew out of Delhi's Indira Gandhi International Airport to Munich on September 4 without clearing immigration, exposing serious gaps in Air India's passenger-handling procedures and prompting the civil aviation ministry to issue a show-cause notice to the airline.

The passengers had travelled from Amritsar to Delhi on Air India flight AI-1115, landing at about 12:50 am on September 4. Roughly an hour later, at around 1:45 am, they boarded Lufthansa flight LH-763 to Munich — without ever passing through the mandatory departure immigration checks, according to a report by The Indian Express, which first broke the story.

How the bypass happened

The incident turns on Air India's "Easy Connect" hub-and-spoke system, under which passengers from select domestic airports flying abroad via a major hub such as Delhi can complete immigration at their point of origin and skip a second check-in in Delhi. Boarding passes for eligible passengers carry a special "I" (international) designator marking them for direct transfer to the international departure gate.

The three Italian nationals were not eligible for that facility. At Amritsar, they were issued "D" (domestic) boarding passes for the Amritsar-Delhi sector — and, in a further breach of procedure, they were also issued boarding passes for their onward Lufthansa flight to Munich at Amritsar itself, before they had even left Punjab. Under the approved standard operating procedure, spoke airports are not meant to issue onward international boarding passes at all.

On arrival in Delhi, the passengers should have been identified as international travellers and diverted from the domestic passenger flow toward immigration at Gate 39. Instead, they were escorted into the airport's international-to-international (I-to-I) transfer area — a zone meant only for passengers who have already cleared immigration and are simply connecting between two international flights. From there, they proceeded directly to the departure zone and boarded the Munich flight.

The ministry's notice flags a further procedural oddity: the boarding pass issued for the Munich leg reportedly fell into neither of the two prescribed categories — "D" or "I" — but a third, unspecified category not provided for under the SOP. Investigators examining the incident attributed the lapse to oversight and confusion, with the passengers mistakenly directed to the departure gate alongside eligible Easy Connect travellers. The breach was discovered only after authorities manually reconciled passenger data.

The ministry's notice

The civil aviation ministry issued the show-cause notice to Air India on September 13, describing the incident as a serious security and immigration-related lapse and giving the airline seven days — until September 20 — to explain why regulatory or administrative action should not be taken for violating the approved SOP governing hub-and-spoke operations. The ministry is examining five specific provisions of Air India's SOPs concerning domestic-international operations, including how the passengers were permitted to enter the international transit area while holding both domestic and onward international tickets.

The fallout has reached the top of the airline. According to LatestLY, the ministry summoned Air India chief executive Campbell Wilson following the incident, underscoring how seriously the government views the procedural failure at the country's busiest airport.

Why it matters for travellers

The hub-and-spoke system was designed to make transits smoother — including for diaspora travellers who routinely fly from smaller Indian cities to international destinations via Delhi. The September 4 lapse shows the system's safeguards depend on ground staff correctly segregating domestic and international passenger flows, and on spoke airports not issuing documents the procedure does not allow.

What to watch

Air India's response to the show-cause notice is due September 20. Beyond any penalty, the incident is likely to force a tightening of the SOPs — and of staff training — at Delhi and at the spoke airports feeding into it, as the ministry moves to close a loophole that let three passengers leave the country with no exit record at all.
